Triggers.value: Physical pain in a part of the body

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I pretend it happened to someone else
constantly check body for signs of danger or injury

Threat.value: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger

Negative Appraisals.value: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again
I feel ashamed of what happened to my body

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Survival Guilt: I feel guilty for surviving when others did not
issues.explanation: 'Survival guilt' implies a trauma context involving deaths of others or a mass-casualty/survivor scenario, which is hard to reconcile with the stated index trauma of sexual assault in the absence of any supporting items about others dying. This is a trauma-type mismatch rather than a merely unusual appraisal.

issues.item: Triggers: Feeling Happy: Feeling happy or relaxed
issues.explanation: 'Feeling happy or relaxed' can function as a trigger in PTSD, but here it is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile: the other triggers are perfume/cologne and body pain, while threat is dominated by touch/startle/flashback phenomena and appraisals focus on emotional numbing and self-reliance. The positive-affect trigger is not impossible, but in this item set it lacks a clear clinical link and looks mismatched to the rest of the formulation.

issues.item: Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
issues.explanation: The flashback item is not inherently implausible for sexual assault PTSD, but in this profile the rest of the network is strongly organized around hypervigilance to touch/body danger and negative appraisals, with no memory items and no trigger-to-memory/threat linkage in the formulation. A full reliving-style flashback can coexist, but here it sits somewhat at odds with the otherwise body/startle-centered pattern and appears insufficiently supported by the surrounding items.

vignette:
Khalid's Story

Khalid was twenty-four when it happened. He had been working as a physical therapist at a clinic in Boston for two years, a job he loved-the precision of it, the way he could see a patient's pain diminish under his careful hands. One evening in late March, after closing up the clinic, he stayed to finish some documentation. A man he did not know well, a senior colleague who had occasionally supervised his work, offered him a ride home. Khalid accepted. In the car, the colleague's demeanor shifted. What began as conversation became coercive, then violent. Khalid was pinned in the passenger seat, overpowered, and assaulted. The man wore a heavy cologne-something woody and expensive-smelling that filled the enclosed space. When it was over, Khalid was dropped on a quiet street three miles from home. He walked in a fog, not fully believing what had occurred, telling himself it was a misunderstanding, that he had misread the situation. He did not report it. He told no one.

For the first few weeks, Khalid functioned. He went to work, treated his patients, came home to his wife Amira. But something had fractured inside him. By summer, he had begun to notice that certain smells-a patient's cologne, a colleague's perfume-would trigger a cascade of panic and disorientation. The scent would transport him back to that car, to the feeling of helplessness, and he would become convinced that his body was no longer safe, that he could not trust his own judgment or physical integrity. When a client wearing a familiar fragrance came in for a session, Khalid would find himself scrutinizing his own body afterward, running his hands over his arms and torso, checking for injury or contamination, as though the assault was still somehow happening to him. He had come to believe that his body had been permanently altered, marked by what had been done to him, and that no amount of washing or checking would ever make him feel whole again.

By autumn, the hypervigilance had intensified. Any unexpected movement in his peripheral vision-a patient shifting position on the treatment table, a colleague approaching from behind-sent a jolt of alarm through him, as if danger were imminent. When Amira reached for him in bed, even gently, he would flinch violently, his nervous system interpreting her touch as a threat. She had begun to withdraw, confused and hurt by his reactions. Khalid found himself retreating into a kind of detachment, a way of stepping outside himself when intrusive memories surfaced. He would think, That happened to someone else, not to me, a mental trick that provided momentary relief but left him feeling hollowed out, disconnected from his own life. Yet the detachment never lasted. The moment would pass, and he would be back in his body, hyperaware of every sensation, every potential danger.

What frightened him most was the conviction that he had lost something irreplaceable-that the person he had been before, capable of feeling joy or desire or trust, was gone forever. This belief fed a vicious cycle. Convinced that he could not rely on himself to stay safe, Khalid began avoiding situations that might trigger memories: he stopped going to the clinic's team lunches, made excuses when Amira wanted to be intimate, and took longer and longer routes home to avoid the street where he had been left. Each avoidance reinforced his sense that the world was dangerous and that his body was a liability. The startle responses grew worse, his body now primed to detect threat everywhere. And when he caught a whiff of cologne on a stranger passing him on the street, or when his own vigilance made him acutely aware of a pain in his shoulder, the cycle would tighten again: the trigger would pull him back into the conviction that his body was permanently damaged, that he could never feel normal again, and that he had to remain hyperalert, constantly monitoring for signs of danger, checking and rechecking his own skin.

Three weeks ago, Amira found him sitting in the dark in their bedroom, unable to articulate what was wrong. She insisted he speak to someone. Khalid finally disclosed the assault to her, and then, reluctantly, to a therapist. He came to this first session carrying the weight of eighteen months of silence, still uncertain whether he could trust anyone-even himself-to help him find his way back.
